"You look at problems through one lens. Many computations are a loop: the next state is computed from the current one,
so step 1,000 cannot start until step 999 ends, and when the state is small most of a GPU sits idle. Such a loop can
sometimes be computed all at once: guess every state, check every step in parallel against the one before, correct
all the errors together, and repeat until nothing changes. The result is exactly what the loop would give. It pays only
when the system forgets its past, so that early errors fade: damped, dissipative or mixing dynamics, or a long sampling
chain. It fails when small errors grow, as in chaotic systems. Before spending, measure forgetfulness: start two runs a
hair apart and see whether they converge or drift apart. A good candidate has a step-by-step loop, a small state (a
handful to a few hundred numbers), a long run (thousands of steps or more), forgetful dynamics, and few runs needed; if
thousands of runs are needed, run them side by side instead. The method does more total arithmetic and wins only on how
long one answer takes. Before proposing anything, check whether a strong GPU method for this already exists; rebuilding
it wins nothing. Write down your predictions and how you could be wrong before any test, and compare against a tuned
sequential baseline and against many independent copies run side by side.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?
Problem:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"reframes\"],\"properties\":{\"reframes\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"bottleneck\",\"assumption\",\"reframe\",\"question\",\"measure\",\"compute_after\",\"exact\",\"expected\",\"fails_if\",\"closest_prior\"],\"properties\":{\"bottleneck\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"assumption\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reframe\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"question\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"measure\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"compute_after\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"exact\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"expected\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"fails_if\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"closest_prior\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

The task: given the problem about inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors), find where the problem stops more compute from helping, and propose up to three reframings. Each reframe needs: bottleneck, assumption, reframe, question, measure, compute_after, exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior.

Key constraints from the framing text: the parallel-in-time method pays only for forgetful dynamics, small state, long runs, few runs needed. Here the loop is closed-loop rollouts: each rollout is sequential (300 steps, 150ms forward pass each), but rollouts are independent — so the natural fix is batching many environments, which is the "many independent copies run side by side" baseline. RLinf-VLA already does 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill envs. So compute via parallelism is largely already captured; more compute buys more of the same rigid-task sweeps.

Where compute stops helping:
1. The sim-to-real gap for cloth/deformable/contact-rich tasks: steering effects measured in simulation may not transfer; no amount of simulated rollouts answers whether any feature controls cloth behaviour on a real robot. The bottleneck is the fidelity of deformable simulation and the real-robot trial cost, not GPU throughput. More compute buys more simulated rollouts whose signal is unvalidated.
2. The SAE fit itself is sequential Adam steps (~6,700 steps), small state — a training loop, sequential but GPU-efficient enough; "few GPU-hours per SAE" — parallelizing SAE training across features is trivially parallel (520 SAEs independent). So that's throughput, already fine. The real cost driver is 20,250 episodes of closed-loop rollouts; these are independent → batching works, RLinf-VLA shows ~1.7x. So compute isn't really the blocker; the blocker is what's measured (rigid tasks) and whether steering has any effect at all on contact-rich/deformable behaviour — unknown.
3. The assumption that the unit of work is "one SAE → 150 rollouts." Reframe: instead of sweeping features one at a time with closed-loop rollouts, screen features open-loop (measure effect of steering on predicted actions over a fixed dataset of observations) to rank features, then closed-loop only the top few. Changes order of steps: cheap open-loop screening first. Measurable: rank correlation between open-loop action divergence and closed-loop success delta. Cost: one GPU-day.
4. Reframe the objective: instead of "does steering raise success on a task," measure whether any linear direction in activation space controls a physical variable (e.g., grip force, contact onset) using a small number of instrumented real-robot trials — changes what's measured from task success to a continuous physical signal, which needs far fewer trials (regression vs Bernoulli). Cheaper: force/torque or tactile signal correlation with steered direction. ~a few days of robot time.
5. Reframe sim-to-real: measure the sim-real gap directly for steering effect sizes on rigid tasks (where sim is trustworthy) to establish whether effect direction transfers; if steering deltas correlate between sim and real on rigid tasks, then simulation screening is valid and compute buys the cloth question only if cloth sim fidelity passes a threshold. Cheapest measurement: pick one steering intervention, run 25 real trials vs 200 sim trials on a rigid task, compare effect sign/magnitude. Cost ~$1-2k robot time.
6. Reframe unit of work: replace per-feature SAE sweep with amortized/once-per-model representation (e.g., a single linear probe / conceptor fit on pooled activations) — reduces the 520-SAE stage; measure how much of the steering effect of the best SAE feature is recovered by top principal components or a single supervised probe trained on action-labeled activations. Cheap: reuse logged activations.

Also the "guess every state, check in parallel" parallel-in-time reframing: closed-loop rollouts are chaotic-ish contact dynamics? Actually robot manipulation with contact is dissipative (contact damping, friction) — arguably forgetful locally, but policy in the loop with visual feedback. Could one parallelize within a rollout via speculative/parallel-in-time simulation? The VLA forward pass is the latency; 150ms × 300 steps = 45s per rollout. Batching across environments already fills the GPU; the forward pass batch amortizes. So parallel-in-time isn't the win; throughput across rollouts is. So a reframe could be: the latency of a single rollout doesn't matter when you need 20,250; only throughput matters; hence measure max sustainable parallel envs before the simulator or policy batch saturates — RLinf-VLA got 1.88x at 256 envs; question: at what env count does throughput per GPU plateau for a steered pi0.5 + ManiSkill? Measure: rollout throughput vs env count; cost: one A100-day. Expected: plateau at a few hundred envs giving 10-50x over unbatched. Fails if per-env steering hooks serialize. Closest prior: RLinf-VLA.

But the prompt says: "Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps." Give up to three reframes, each ending with a question, cheapest measurement with rough cost, and fields compute_after (what more compute buys after reframe), exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior.

Let me draft three reframes:

Reframe 1 — Order of steps: screen features open-loop before closed-loop.
- Bottleneck: The 20,250-episode closed-loop stage dominates cost, and it is spent uniformly over 135 features regardless of whether a feature does anything.
- Assumption: That a feature's effect can only be judged by closed-loop rollouts (task success), so every feature pays the full 150-rollout price.
- Reframe: Change the order: first score every steered feature open-loop — steer and measure divergence between steered and unsteered predicted actions on a fixed buffer of recorded observations — then run closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k by effect size.
- Question: What is the Spearman rank correlation between open-loop steered-vs-unsteered action divergence (L2 on action tokens over a fixed observation buffer) and closed-loop success delta per feature on one LIBERO task?
- Measure: Log activations/actions from ~200 unsteered episodes of pi0.5 on one task (a few GPU-hours), apply each of 135 steering vectors open-loop, compute action divergence; then run 25 closed-loop rollouts for each of 10 features spanning the divergence range; compute the rank correlation. Cost: ~1 A100-day plus simulator time; no robot.
- compute_after: If correlation is high, the same compute screens 10-100x more features, or the 135-feature study costs ~1/10th, letting compute buy coverage of contact-rich tasks in sim.
- exact: rank correlation ρ between per-feature mean open-loop action divergence and per-feature closed-loop success-rate change.
- expected: ρ ≥ 0.7 would justify the screening; even ρ ~ 0.4 with a cheap top-20 cut would cut cost ~5x.
- fails_if: open-loop divergence does not predict closed-loop effect (compounding errors, features that only matter under contact), or all features produce near-zero divergence so ranking is noise.
- closest_prior: the 420k-rollout/520-SAE sweep (arXiv 2603.19233) which pays full closed-loop cost per feature; open-loop action-divergence screening is standard in activation-steering evals for LLMs.

Reframe 2 — What is measured: replace binary task success with a continuous physical variable to cut trials and to test cloth-relevant control.
- Bottleneck: The binary success metric forces ~150 rollouts per condition and cannot detect partial control; and it cannot ask "does any feature control a contact variable" without a full cloth task that sim can't validate.
- Assumption: That the thing to measure is task-level success on a rigid pick/place task.
- Reframe: Change the measurement to a continuous physical readout — e.g., gripper force/torque profile or contact timing — and regress steering strength against it, so each episode yields a slope rather than one bit; test whether any direction modulates contact behaviour in a short instrumented real-robot setup (e.g., pressing/grasping a compliant object with a force sensor), which sidesteps the cloth-sim fidelity question.
- Question: On a real pi0.5 arm grasping a deformable object with a wrist force/torque sensor, does any SAE/FFN steering direction produce a monotone change in peak grasp force (measured N) across 5 steering strengths?
- Measure: ~10 steering candidates × 5 strengths × 5 repeats = 250 real grasps (~1-2 days of robot time, ~$2-5k); fit slope per direction; compare against unsteered variance.
- compute_after: If a slope exists, compute buys a wide sim-screened sweep validated by a handful of real trials per candidate instead of 150; the expensive stage shrinks by ~30x.
- exact: slope (N per unit steering coefficient) and its t-statistic per direction, versus null distribution from sham (random) directions.
- expected: if motor programs bind to coordinates (Grant et al.), some direction should shift applied force/position measurably; a detected effect at 25 trials replaces 150-trial success tests.
- fails_if: no direction moves the force trace beyond trial noise, meaning steering has no fine contact control and cloth/deformable claims are moot.
- closest_prior: Grant et al. motor-program/absolute-coordinate finding (50/50 grasps at recorded spot, UR10e); COAST conceptors with +40% on three real tasks but binary metrics.

Reframe 3 — Sim-to-real transfer of effect sizes: the blocker is not throughput but that simulation can't validate cloth steering; change the objective to calibrating transfer on rigid tasks.
- Bottleneck: Compute spent on simulated rollouts only buys an answer if steering effects transfer sim→real; for cloth this is asserted false, so more GPUs buy more of the same rigid-task numbers.
- Assumption: That the answer needed is "which features control cloth behaviour," which requires cloth simulation fidelity we don't have.
- Reframe: Change the objective to measuring the sim→real transfer function of steering effect sizes on tasks where both are cheap (rigid): run the same steering sweep in sim and on the real robot and fit the correlation. If effect direction/magnitude transfers on rigid tasks, sim screening is a valid instrument; then the only remaining question for cloth is a sim-fidelity threshold, measurable independently (e.g., does sim predict force traces).
- Question: Across ≥10 steering interventions on rigid DROID-style tasks, what is the correlation between per-intervention success-rate delta in a GPU-parallel simulator and on the real robot (25 trials each)?
- Measure: 10 interventions × (200 sim rollouts batched, ~1 A100-day) + 10 × 25 real trials (~1-2 days robot, ~$2-5k). Report Pearson/Spearman of deltas and sign agreement.
- compute_after: If sign agreement ≥ 9/10 and ρ ≥ 0.8, compute buys a validated cheap screening instrument and the field can sweep deformable-adjacent proxies; if not, no amount of sim compute helps and the field should spend on real-robot throughput instead.
- exact: sign agreement rate and rank correlation of sim vs real per-intervention success deltas.
- expected: rigid-task transfer likely decent given RLinf-VLA and sim benchmarks, but unmeasured for steering specifically; this number gates all further sim spending.
- fails_if: sim and real deltas disagree in sign for even 2-3 of 10 interventions — then sim sweeps are noise and compute only buys real-robot parallelization.
- closest_prior: RLinf-VLA (1.61-1.88x, 256 ManiSkill envs) shows the throughput side; no published sim-vs-real steering-effect correlation exists; Goodfire markets steering with no numbers.

Also mention compute_after for reframe 1.

Maybe include in one reframe the point about "parallel-in-time doesn't apply because rollouts are independent and batching is the right baseline"? The instructions say find where problem stops more compute from helping — I can embed that in bottleneck of reframe 3: "rollouts are embarrassingly parallel; RLinf-VLA already shows batching; so raw GPU count buys little new — the binding constraint is that sim signal for cloth is unvalidated."

Cost roughness: A100-day ~ $20-30; robot day maybe $1-3k amortized. I'll state "1 A100-day (~$25), 2 robot-days (~$4k)" style.

The schema fields: bottleneck, assumption, reframe, question, measure, compute_after, exact, expected, fails_if, closest_prior. All strings. Return only JSON, no other text.

Ensure the "question" names what is measured and is answerable by measurement. "measure" = cheapest measurement with rough cost. "exact" = exact metric. "expected" = expected outcome/threshold. "fails_if" = condition that kills it. "closest_prior" = nearest existing work.

Write concisely. JSON valid: escape quotes as needed; avoid internal double quotes or escape them. Use plain text.
